title: Seahawks sale proves NFL franchise values will 'keep going up' | Dan Patrick Show | NFL on NBC
text: Ben Horny works for Front Office Sports, a reporter. He covers deals, finance, private equity, ownership. Ben, we thought of you when we saw where Seattle went for $9.6 billion. What was your reaction to that purchase price? >> Yeah, Dan, thanks for having me on. And I wish someone told me what color shirt you were going to wear. Uh very you know, historic price. Um My thought was that it was in line with what I expected. You know, this it was an interesting process because who you spoke to, people thought this was either going to shatter the record, we were going to be over 10 billion, you know, or it was going to be in the 8 billion range. Pretty close to 10 billion, so it's not quite the Lakers sale, but it's the second highest pro sports team, you know, sale ever. >> But you get the building, whereas the Broncos sale, they didn't get the building. >> Yes, and that is a I mean, that's a major component in any of these deals, right? And I think we might get into it a little bit later, but I think if you're trying to prognostic who's going to sell, um that's one of the aspects you want to look at, you know, what's the deal with the stadium. These things cost a lot of money. Uh upgrades cost a lot of money, new arenas cost a lot of money. Um so, having that be part of the deal is a big a big deal, yeah. >> Okay, is $9.6 billion a good investment? >> It seems like it. You know, from everyone that I talked to, NFL franchise valuations in particular, they're just going to keep going up. Uh and I mean, the same goes for the NBA as well. It's hasn't been quite the same level in the NHL and MLB, although people expect once there's some certainty on this labor situation with Major League Baseball that that will change. Uh but you know, I keep asking people, what's the tipping point? [clears throat] When is this going to peak? Uh and I'm told that that's not happening yet. So, I would not be shocked uh if there's another NFL franchise that, you know, goes for 10 billion plus in the future. >> But if that's the case, then why would anybody want to sell the franchise if it's just going to continue to go up? >> It's a great question. You know, NFL franchises cost a lot of money to run. So, to your question about whether it's a good investment, I mean, it is. These are great team Not only are they trophy assets, but NFL franchises make a lot of money, but you also have to spend a lot of money, and not just on player salary, which is a huge component of it, but it's like I said before, stadium upgrades, I mean, concessions, uh there are all kinds of, you know, it's it's complicated to run a team. So, I think some people get burnt out. I think there's tax implications for some of these people who don't want to just leave the team to their family, uh which that kind of used to be how it it worked. Um so, yeah. >> Uh the most valuable NFL team right now is >> I mean, I think you have to say the Dallas Cowboys. Yeah, I I I'm not going to I wouldn't guess what their uh value is, because frankly, the value is whatever someone's willing to pay. I have no sense that Jerry Jones intends to sell the team, uh but yeah, if the Cowboys ever went up for sale, it would shatter the record, no question. >> Uh the next team that you think will be sold. >> That's another great question. Uh you know, I could make a wild guess. I don't have any uh particular insight. Uh again, there's a lot of reasons to stay in the NFL business, but uh you know, there's maybe some older owners, uh you know, the Browns come to mind, uh but I don't, you know, again, these are wild speculations. >> Least valuable NFL team is who? >> Least valuable NFL team? That's also a difficult one. They all are multi-billion dollar franchises. Uh even I mean again, I'm not trying to hate on the Browns here, but even the Browns who get clowned on a lot, if they were put up for sale, I mean they're most likely breaking the Commanders record of 6.05 billion, which now is, you know, that was I think it's like six This deal was 60% higher than the Commanders sale, which was only a few years ago. text: Tuesday July 14th edition of PFT PM. Got a lot to get to today and I want to start with the All-Star game. The Major League Baseball All-Star game, which once upon a time for me became the center of the summer universe. I loved it. I couldn't get enough of it. I went to two of them, 1988 and 1994. In 1994, went to the home run derby, used to be in the afternoon on the Monday. And there was just something that was always special, magical, riveting, especially because they didn't have interleague play except for the World Series. You rarely got to see the collection of the best of one league against the best that you never got to see it except in the World Series and the rosters top to bottom weren't nearly as good as the All-Star rosters. And it's just amazing how it just doesn't have anything close to the pizzazz it used to have. I didn't watch any of the home run derby, none of it. Not interested in it. Never was all that intrigued by it. Guys hitting home runs, kids out in the outfield catching them. It's kind of like fireworks. You get to a point where I've seen enough. I know how it goes. Ooh, ball goes out of the stadium. Ooh, ball almost goes out of the stadium. We get it. They hit home runs. But it's just amazing for me over 30 years how it's gone from something that was such a central part of the summer experience to something that I don't even pay attention to. And it was always a fun time when I was a kid because my dad, the bookie, he had two days off during the course of the year. The day before and the day after the All-Star game. Those were the only two days at the time when there was nothing else going on in the sports world, at least the sports world that people wanted to bet on. There is some All-Star related news that landed on the radar screen. Now, this popped up on Friday. The report from the Philadelphia Inquirer that Philly's first baseman Bryce Harper had recorded a video that had been purchased by a FanDuel VIP host for one of the FanDuel customers. And we know how the news cycles go. If something happens on a Friday if you get through the weekend, there's often a hard reset and and it's forgotten because we move on constantly. I said yesterday, one week felt like a year with all the stuff that happens that we're paying attention to. And it's easy to forget things that happened last week because so much happens in any given week. Harper issued a statement yesterday, and I think that it's an indication that he realizes this isn't some small issue. He mentions that he has a lawyer for this specific purpose, which either means he's going to sue somebody or he's concerned about getting sued or generally landing in a jackpot. If you're watching this, there is the full statement from Bryce Harper with his position regarding the video that was purchased through Cameo by a person named Britney who wanted a holiday video for a gentleman named Terry. Now, Terry, it turns out, is a compulsive gambler who is suing multiple sports books and the NFL for the praying upon him by the use of the micro betting. And Harper added this, and this is what to me is key. He shows the script that was used. Now, his general position is I didn't know FanDuel was going to use this for business purposes. Dude, look at the script. When the host from FanDuel is the person providing the message as a Thanksgiving gift. Side note, who the hell gives Thanksgiving gifts anyway? Thanksgiving is not a time for gift, it's a time for gluttony. That's it. It's an eating holiday. It's not a gift holiday. So, Bryce Harper's trying to thread this needle very clumsily that he had no idea FanDuel was going to use this for promotional purposes, was going to use it for business purposes. There's a separate category of videos that are purchased through Cameo for business purposes. What the hell did he think he was doing when he saw the script? Now, FanDuel was wrong to put its logo on the video, but what does he think a FanDuel host is? Why does he think that a FanDuel host would be buying something for someone? It puts you on notice as Bryce Harper that this may be part of the effort to keep Terry spending his money and losing his money through FanDuel. And that's really why I've been covering this. The NFL got lucky on this one that it wasn't an Eagles player, it was a Phillies player that got caught up in this. First of all, when you made the money that Bryce Harper's made, what What you doing on Cameo? They contacted me about Cameo years ago and they explained it to me. I I No. No, I No. I No. And you're taking half of this? I'm going to do these videos and we're splitting it 50/50 just cuz you have the the infrastructure in place to allow this. No, not interested. And I don't know, maybe some people are making a lot of money doing it, but when you've made the kind of money Bryce Harper's made, why the hell are you doing this? Why are you doing it? And now he's in a jackpot. And it's more of a PR mess right now, I think, than anything else. his claims, I reject them. They're not persuasive. The script makes it clear to you that someone from FanDuel bought this thing. FanDuel host is all that you need for the red flag to go up, for the alarms to sound. At a minimum FanDuel's trying to circumvent the higher prices that go with business videos. At worst this is something that they're using to keep a loser losing. And that's really the message here. And wait, we've known for years about what happens when you go to Las Vegas. If you're getting free stuff, that means you're losing. And the nicer the stuff you're getting at the hotel, the bigger the suite the bigger the bath you've been taking in the casino. you got to go to Vegas to be treated that way. You got to get there to this geographic location. This new world of giving you free stuff, it goes everywhere. It's tentacles are everywhere because it's all tied into your phone. The more you bet, the more you lose, the more they want to try to keep you betting and losing, so they start treating you like any other business that provides a service will treat its customers. You get gifts. You get perks. You get perks that are partially paid for by all the money you've lost. It's just another reason why there's so much regulation that is needed in that industry. We are firmly in the Wild West phase where everybody is grabbing as much money as they can before the reckoning comes, and the reckoning can't get here soon enough because people are having their lives turned upside down. They're being preyed upon with the advertising, being preyed upon with these tactics to keep them betting even when they're trying to disengage. Every time they think they're out, they pull them back in with the Bryce Harper video. So, we're going to keep covering it. And hey, if any of the sportsbooks out there don't like it, change your ways cuz you're not doing a good enough job of regulating yourselves cuz you're creating these issues. These issues are popping up, and usually when you hear about one, there's more that we're not hearing about. The regulations are needed. The industry needs to be cleaned up. We need to get past the Wild West phase to the reckoning phase and the regulation phase so everybody understands the whole thing a little bit better. I'm trying to be one of the voices that explains to people you're not going to get rich. You're not going to pay your bills, and if you think that's what's going to happen, you're going to end up not living in your house. You're going to end up relocating to that vague thing we always were afraid of in the '70s, the poorhouse. Whatever and wherever the poorhouse is, you didn't want to go there. All right. To the NFL. And I'll have more to say about the World Cup tomorrow. You know, by the way, there's a pretty important match today between France and Spain at AT&T Stadium in Dallas. Not AT&T Stadium. And then tomorrow it's England and Argentina. Two significant matches over the next 2 days. No World Cup update today other than to remind you of what's coming. To the NFL, here's what's coming for Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson. And I think at the surface level, there's been a lot of confusion about where he stands as it relates to a recent arrest on felony domestic battery charges. The authorities have been saying repeatedly in recent days that he's not going to face criminal charges. And the item yesterday from ESPN that leads with Jackson won't be prosecuted for a felony. The important part from the NFL's perspective is this. The spokesperson for the LA City Attorney's Office indicated that the case is going to be referred to a program in which certain people who could be charged with misdemeanors are eligible for a diversionary program. that's important because the NFL under the personal conduct policy, the finding of a violation is very broad. It's not just convicted at trial. It's not just plead guilty. It's not just no contest plea. It's any resolution other than you walk away with no charges whatsoever and no acknowledgement directly or indirectly of any responsibility. Your life changes in no way. You just go free. And it's gone forever. It's like it never existed. A diversion program is specifically identified in the personal conduct policy as one of the things that constitutes a violation of the policy. If you enter a diversion program as a way to resolve potential charges, boom, it's a violation. They don't even need to investigate. The diversion program is the violation. And if I recall correctly, and there's a good chance I don't. I think the Ray Rice tornado that nearly took out the commissioner in 2014, that started with a diversion program, too. And he emerged with a two-game suspension. And everybody was dismayed. I remember the commissioner being at the Hall of Fame game that year, being chased around by reporters who wanted to press him on why only two games when Ray Rice allegedly rendered his then-fiancée unconscious in an elevator at an Atlantic City casino. And then came the video. But I think that all started with a diversion program. The fact that Alaric Jackson apparently is on track to avoid a misdemeanor prosecution by entering a diversion program means he will have violated the personal conduct policy. And since the underlying allegation is domestic battery, that sets up a baseline suspension of six games. because he's already been suspended under the personal conduct policy once, two game suspension, couple of years ago, that sets him up for enhanced penalties, aggravating factors for a second violation. So, unless you really dig into this, when you may have the impression, "Oh, not an issue. He'll be available all year long." When they have repeat offenders, they expedite the process. I fully expect that this thing will move quickly. I fully expect there'll be another suspension. And it'll probably more than six games this time around for Alaric Jackson. So, just because he's not facing the possibility of a felony conviction and the prison time that would go along with that, He's still facing a suspension. And remember this, even though the current process involves Judge Sue L. Robinson, who has the hearing and determines what happened and then issues the punishment, they can be appealed to the commissioner. The findings made by Judge Sue L. Robinson can never be appealed. Well, the findings are irrelevant here because the violation is the diversion program. Her role only becomes important when there's nothing that the criminal process is done. When a person wasn't prosecuted at all, the NFL does its own investigation like what happened with Deshaun Watson. He didn't face charges. Grand jury did not indict him. But the process went forward and he ended up with an 11-game suspension. When you enter a diversion program, that part of it's done. All that matters is the punishment, and the punishment ultimately gets appealed to the I will not be surprised. I'm not making any predictions here. I'm not making any reports. title: Could Rams LT Alaric Jackson face another suspension? | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: to the NFL. Here's what's coming for Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson. And I think at the surface level, there's been a lot of confusion about where he stands as it relates to a recent arrest on felony domestic battery charges. The authorities have been saying repeatedly in recent days that he's not going to face criminal charges. And the item yesterday from ESPN that leads with Jackson won't be prosecuted for a felony. The important part from the NFL's perspective is this. The spokesperson for the LA City Attorney's office indicated that the case is going to be referred to a program in which certain people who could be charged with misdemeanors are eligible for a diversionary program. And that's important because the NFL under the personal conduct policy, the finding of a violation is very broad. It's not just convicted at trial. It's not just plead guilty. It's not just no contest plea. It's any resolution other than you walk away with no charges whatsoever and no acknowledgement directly or indirectly of any responsibility. Your life changes in no way. You just go free. And it's gone forever. It's like it never existed. A diversion program is specifically identified in the personal conduct policy as one of the things that constitutes a violation of the policy. If you enter a diversion program as a way to resolve potential charges, boom, it's a violation. They don't even need to investigate. The diversion program is the violation. And if I recall correctly, and there's a good chance I don't, I think the Ray Rice tornado that nearly took out the commissioner in 2014, that started with a diversion program, too. And he emerged with a two-game suspension. And everybody was dismayed. I remember the commissioner being at the Hall of Fame game that year, being chased around by reporters who wanted to press him on why only two games when Ray Rice allegedly rendered his then fiance unconscious in an elevator at an Atlantic City casino. And then came the video. But I think that all started with a diversion program. The fact that Alaric Jackson apparently is on track to avoid a misdemeanor prosecution by entering a diversion program means he will have violated the personal conduct policy. And since the underlying allegation is domestic battery, that sets up a baseline suspension of six games. because he's already been suspended under the personal conduct policy once, two game suspension, couple of years ago, that sets him up for enhanced penalties, aggravating factors for a second violation. So, unless you really dig into this when you may have the impression, "Oh, not an issue. He'll be available all year long." When they have repeat offenders, they expedite the process. I fully expect that this thing will move quickly. I fully expect there'll be another And it'll probably more than six games this time around for Alaric Jackson. So, just because he's not facing the possibility of a felony conviction and the prison time that would go along with that, he's still facing a suspension. And remember this, even though the current process involves Judge Sue L. Robinson, who has the hearing and determines what happened and then issues the punishment, they can be appealed to the commissioner. The findings made by Judge Sue L. Robinson can never be appealed. Well, the findings are irrelevant here because the violation is the diversion program. Her role only becomes important when there's nothing that the criminal process has done. When a person wasn't prosecuted at all, the NFL does its own investigation, like what happened with Deshaun Watson. He didn't face charges. Grand jury did not indict him. But the process went forward and he ended up with 11-game suspension. When you enter a diversion program, that part of it's done. All that matters is the punishment, and the punishment ultimately gets appealed to the I will not be surprised. I'm not making any predictions here. I'm not making any reports. I won't be surprised if Alaric Jackson doesn't make the trip to Australia with the Rams for the week one game against the 49ers. All right, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. title: Discussing Bryce Harper's statement regarding 2024 Cameo Video | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: There is some All-Star related news that landed on the radar screen. Now, this popped up on Friday. The report from the Philadelphia Inquirer that Phillies first baseman Bryce Harper had recorded a video that had been purchased by a FanDuel VIP host for one of the FanDuel customers. I said yesterday, one week felt like a year with all the stuff that happens that we're paying attention to. And it's easy to forget things that happened last week because so much happens in any given week. Harper issued a statement yesterday, and I think that it's an indication that he realizes this isn't some small issue. He mentions that he has a lawyer for this specific purpose, which either means he's going to sue somebody or he's concerned about getting sued or generally landing in a jackpot. If you're watching this, there is the full statement from Bryce Harper with his position regarding the video that was purchased through Cameo by a person named Brittany who wanted a holiday video for a gentleman named Terry. Now, Terry, it turns out, is a compulsive gambler who is suing multiple sports books and the NFL for the preying upon him by the use of the micro betting. And Harper added this, and this is what to me is key. He shows the script that was used. Now, his general position is I didn't know FanDuel was going to use this for business purposes. Dude, look at the script. When the host from FanDuel is the person providing the message as a Thanksgiving gift. Side note, who the hell gives Thanksgiving gifts anyway? Thanksgiving is not a time for gift, it's a time for gluttony. That's it. It's an eating holiday. It's not a gift holiday. So, Bryce Harper's trying to thread this needle very clumsily that he had no idea FanDuel was going to use this for promotional purposes, was going to use it for business purposes. There's a separate category of videos that are purchased through Cameo for business purposes. What the hell did he think he was doing when he saw the script? Now, FanDuel was wrong to put its logo on the video, but what does he think a FanDuel host is? Why does he think that a FanDuel host would be buying something for someone? It puts you on notice as Bryce Harper that this may be part of the effort to keep Terry spending his money and losing his money through FanDuel. And that's really why I've been covering this. The NFL got lucky on this one that it wasn't an Eagles player, it was a Phillies player that got caught up in this. First of all, when you made the money that Bryce Harper's made, what are you doing on Cameo? They contacted me about Cameo years ago, and they explained it to me. I No. No, I No. I No. And you're taking half of this? I'm going to do these videos and we're splitting it 50/50 just cuz you have the the infrastructure in place to allow this. No, not interested. And I don't know, maybe some people are making a lot of money doing it, but when you've made the kind of money Bryce Harper's made, why the hell are you doing this? Why are you doing it? And now he's in a jackpot. And it's more of a PR mess right now, I think, than anything else. But his claims, I reject them. They're not persuasive. The script makes it clear to you that someone from FanDuel bought this thing. FanDuel host is all that you need for the red flag to go up, for the alarms to sound. At a minimum, FanDuel's trying to circumvent the higher prices that go with business videos. At worst, this is something that they're using to keep a loser losing. And that's really the message here. And wait, we've known for years about what happens when you go to Las Vegas. If you're getting free stuff, that means you're losing. And the nicer the stuff you're getting at the hotel, the bigger the suite, the bigger the bath you've been taking in the casino. you got to go to Vegas to be treated that way. You got to get there to this geographic location. This new world of giving you free stuff, it goes everywhere. It's tentacles are everywhere because it's all tied into your phone. The more you bet, the more you lose, the more they want to try to keep you betting and losing, so they start treating you like any other business that provides a service will treat its customers. You get gifts. You get perks. You get perks that are partially paid for by all the money you've lost. It's just another reason why there's so much regulation that is needed in that industry. We are firmly in the wild west phase where everybody is grabbing as much money as they can before the reckoning comes, and the reckoning can't get here soon enough because people are having their lives turned upside down. They're being preyed upon with the advertising, they're being preyed upon with these tactics to keep them betting even when they're trying to disengage. Every time they think they're out, they pull them back in with the Bryce Harper video. So, we're going to keep covering it. And hey, if any of the sports books out there don't like it, change your ways cuz you're not doing a good enough job of regulating yourselves cuz you're creating these issues. These issues are popping up and usually when you hear about one, there's more that we're not hearing about. The regulations are needed, the industry needs to be cleaned up, we need to get past the wild west phase to the reckoning phase, and the regulation phase so everybody understands the whole thing a little bit better. I'm trying to be one of the voices that explains to people you're not going to get rich, you're not going to pay your bills, and if you think that's what's going to happen, you're going to end up not living in your house, you're going to end up relocating to that vague thing we always were afraid of in the '70s, the poor house. Whatever and wherever the poor house is, you didn't want to go there. All right, it's Mike Florio, thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. title: ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler Talks NFL QB Rankings & More with Rich Eisen | Full Interview

text: in advance of the launch of his new leadership podcast series, Coach to Coach, which will debut with episodes dropping on Wednesday, uh, with the Super Bowl champion and Hall of Fame head coach to Tony Dunie. I >> Oh, yeah. He used to have this great clapper. You know, we're doing this leadership podcast and one of the things we talk about a lot is the energy of the leader pervades the group. So, you know, if you're positive with with players when good things happen and when you're positive with them, you know, when bad things happen to help them get through it, uh, you know, I think those are good things to allow them to play well. >> Is there a through line? because again I I future episodes with Andy Reid, Shawn Payeyton, uh Dan Campbell, Joe Madden of the uh Cubs, Joe Gerardi as well, just to name a handful of them. Uh a throughine was there a general a a general sense that you picked up a consensus about coaching, managing Jason at all? Oh, I think there are so many things that I've learned from this experience. And you know, the the big takeaway for me is how generous these guys are. They're obviously the best at what they do. Uh so many of them have won Super Bowls or World Series, won championships, and you know, at the core of them, they're just coaches. They they want to help players get better. They want to build teams that they're all proud to be a part of. And for me, that's what I always thought about when I was coaching. So, they were really fun conversations to have. We talk a lot about some of the challenging times they had and what they learned from those experiences and they share those stories. And you know, one of the things I learned in I've learned in TV is that people just don't want to hear platitudes. As the great Fred Gadelli said, enough of the platitudes. So, you know, people want stories and they want points to the story. And when I coached, I used to always tell our players stories and then, you know, hopefully they remember them and then, okay, why am I telling you this? And and that's a big part of what these shows have been is uh is these coaches taking us through different experiences they've had, different influences they've had, and sharing those things with us. And then, hey, what did I learn from that? What was the lesson learned from that experience? Good, bad, or indifferent. So, uh, you know, we do these, they're they're about an hour long and and I tell every one of them I could go for three, four, five hours with them because I learned so much. >> Yeah. A coach tocoachpodcast.com uh to check out again uh coach to coach or wherever you get your podcast. Jason Garrett here on the Rich Eisen Show. You just said uh seconds ago um that you used to tell stories to players to try and you know I guess coach them up or give them perspective. What story did you tell Dak Prescott in 2016 when suddenly he was thrust to the four of everything for your team Jason? >> Well uh you know I probably learned as much from him that he learned from from us and and and I'll tell you that story. uh you know, he came in, we drafted him in the fourth round and and and my thought when we drafted him was, hey, this guy can be the next quarterback of the Cowboys. There's no doubt in my mind about that. But my biggest concern was was the initial trans transition because he had been a gun quarterback, a lot of quarterback runs at Mississippi State. Um, you know, the biggest thing I've tried to do is develop relationships wi with the guys. It's it's easier on the offensive side of the ball, more difficult on the defensive side of the ball, but he would play chess with some of the defensive guys. And not to bring up any bad memories, but I've always been curious, what did the officials tell you on the sideline after Dez Bryant caught it, but then didn't in that playoff game prior to Dak's time? Obviously, Romo threw that one and your decision to go for it in the whole thing. Jason, >> yeah, it was uh it was really interesting to me. De uh Dean Blandino obviously was the guy back in the booth at the time and and Jean Ster was the was the game official. And uh as you remember um it was called a catch on the field and uh you know there was always a question of okay how long does someone have to possess the ball in order for it to be a catch? And if I heard the the the official say it once, I literally heard him say it a thousand times. You know, it was time enough to make a football move. Time enough to make a football move. And then they'd be very clear with you. They say they don't even have to make a football move. It just they just need time enough to make a football move. And so that was ringing in my head as I saw Dez Bryant catch this ball in about the sixyd line in the air and switch the ball >> and get one, two, three down, take the ball here, lunge and extend it to the goal line and then the ball comes out.
